items.name: Repair Windows system files
items.summary: For crashes, errors about missing files, or Windows features that stopped working. Checks Windows' own files and replaces damaged ones.
items.effect: Only damaged Windows files are replaced. It can take a long time and may ask for a restart. When it ends, the files that were repaired or could not be repaired are listed in the output.
sources: Microsoft Support: System File Checker (DISM first, then SFC; the [SR] lines of CBS.log)

options.label: Create a restore point first
options.detail: Windows allows one restore point every 24 hours, and System Protection must be on for the system drive (the Create a restore point fix can turn it on). If it declines, the repair goes on and the output says why.

options.label: Also clean up old update files afterwards
options.detail: Frees some space; old updates can no longer be uninstalled.

steps.title: Create a restore point
args: $ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop'; try { $before = @(Microsoft.PowerShell.Management\Get-ComputerRestorePoint -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue); $known = @($before | Microsoft.PowerShell.Core\ForEach-Object { $_.SequenceNumber }); Microsoft.PowerShell.Management\Checkpoint-Computer -Description 'TidyWindow: before repairing Windows files' -RestorePointType MODIFY_SETTINGS -WarningVariable skipped -WarningAction SilentlyContinue; $added = @(Microsoft.PowerShell.Management\Get-ComputerRestorePoint -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Microsoft.PowerShell.Core\Where-Object { $known -notcontains $_.SequenceNumber }); if ($added.Count -gt 0) { 'Restore point created.'; exit 0 }; if ($skipped) { "$skipped" }; $latest = $before | Microsoft.PowerShell.Utility\Sort-Object SequenceNumber | Microsoft.PowerShell.Utility\Select-Object -Last 1; if ($latest) { $made = [Management.ManagementDateTimeConverter]::ToDateTime($latest.CreationTime); if (((Microsoft.PowerShell.Utility\Get-Date) - $made).TotalHours -lt 24) { 'No new restore point was needed. Windows allows one every 24 hours, and the one named ' + $latest.Description + ' was made on ' + $made.ToString('f') + '. You can go back to that one.'; exit 0 } }; 'Windows did not create a restore point. System Protection is probably off for the system drive, or the space for restore points is full. Turn it on with the Create a restore point fix, or in System Properties > System Protection.'; exit 1 } catch { $_.Exception.Message; exit 2 }

steps.title: List the files SFC repaired or could not repair
args: $ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop'; $file = "$env:SystemRoot\Logs\CBS\CBS.log"; if (-not [System.IO.File]::Exists($file)) { 'CBS.log was not found, so there is no list of files to show.'; exit 0 }; $stream = [System.IO.File]::Open($file, 'Open', 'Read', 'ReadWrite'); try { $null = $stream.Seek(-[Math]::Min($stream.Length, 48MB), 'End'); $reader = [System.IO.StreamReader]::new($stream); $found = [System.Collections.Generic.List[string]]::new(); $begin = ''; while ($null -ne ($line = $reader.ReadLine())) { if ($line.Contains('[SR] Beginning Verify and Repair')) { $found.Clear(); $begin = $line.Substring(0, [Math]::Min(19, $line.Length)); continue }; if ($begin -and $line -match '\[SR\] (Cannot repair|Repairing corrupted|Repairing \d+ components|Repair complete|Verify complete|Verifying \d+ components)') { $found.Add($(if ($line.Length -gt 300) { $line.Substring(0, 300) } else { $line })) } } } finally { $stream.Dispose() }; if (-not $begin) { 'No System File Checker scan was found in the log.'; exit 0 }; 'The last System File Checker scan in the log began at ' + $begin + '.'; $cannot = @($found | Microsoft.PowerShell.Core\Where-Object { $_ -match 'Cannot repair' }); $fixed = @($found | Microsoft.PowerShell.Core\Where-Object { $_ -match 'Repairing corrupted' }); $found | Microsoft.PowerShell.Utility\Select-Object -First 80; if ($cannot.Count -gt 0) { 'Windows could not repair ' + $cannot.Count + ' file(s). The lines above name them.'; exit 1 }; if ($fixed.Count -gt 0) { 'Windows repaired ' + $fixed.Count + ' file(s).' } else { 'No damaged files were found in that scan.' }

items.name: Reset Windows Update
items.summary: For updates that fail, get stuck downloading, or never finish checking. Stops the update services, clears what they downloaded, and starts them again.
items.effect: Downloaded update files are renamed to .bak and the Delivery Optimization cache is emptied (Windows downloads them again). Your installed updates are not removed. If something has turned one of the update services off, the fix says so and stops: it never changes how a service starts. Afterwards open Settings > Windows Update and check for updates.
sources: Microsoft Learn: Reset Windows Update components manually
WinUtil (cross-check; its policy clean-up was not copied)

options.label: Also reset the update database and certificate store
options.detail: Use only if the first try did not help. The list of past updates in Settings starts empty.

steps.title: Remove the old download queue files
Set aside the downloaded update files
Set aside the update certificate store

items.name: Check the drive for errors
items.summary: For slow or freezing PCs, files that will not open, or strange crashes. Reads the health, wear and error counts of your drives and scans the system drive for problems.
items.effect: Nothing is changed; this only reads and reports. If errors are reported, open an administrator Command Prompt and run chkdsk C: /f; Windows repairs the drive at the next restart.
sources: Microsoft Learn: Repair-Volume -Scan (an online scan that changes nothing); Get-StorageReliabilityCounter

steps.title: Read drive health
args: Storage\Get-PhysicalDisk | Microsoft.PowerShell.Utility\Select-Object FriendlyName, MediaType, HealthStatus, OperationalStatus | Microsoft.PowerShell.Utility\Format-Table -AutoSize | Microsoft.PowerShell.Utility\Out-String -Width 120

steps.title: Read drive wear, temperature and error counts
args: $ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop'; $rows = @(Storage\Get-PhysicalDisk | Microsoft.PowerShell.Core\ForEach-Object { $c = $_ | Storage\Get-StorageReliabilityCounter; [pscustomobject]@{ Drive = $_.FriendlyName; Temperature = $c.Temperature; WearPercent = $c.Wear; PowerOnHours = $c.PowerOnHours; ReadErrors = $c.ReadErrorsUncorrected; WriteErrors = $c.WriteErrorsUncorrected } }); $rows | Microsoft.PowerShell.Utility\Format-List | Microsoft.PowerShell.Utility\Out-String -Width 140; 'A blank means the drive does not report that figure. WearPercent is how much of the life of an SSD is used.'; $bad = @($rows | Microsoft.PowerShell.Core\Where-Object { $_.ReadErrors -gt 0 -or $_.WriteErrors -gt 0 -or $_.WearPercent -ge 90 }); if ($bad.Count -gt 0) { 'A drive reports uncorrected errors or is nearly worn out. Back up what matters to you.'; exit 1 }

steps.title: Read the system drive’s health
args: $ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop'; Storage\Get-Volume -DriveLetter $env:SystemDrive.Substring(0, 1) | Microsoft.PowerShell.Utility\Select-Object DriveLetter, FileSystemType, HealthStatus, OperationalStatus, @{ Name = 'FreeGB'; Expression = { [math]::Round($_.SizeRemaining / 1GB, 1) } }, @{ Name = 'SizeGB'; Expression = { [math]::Round($_.Size / 1GB, 1) } } | Microsoft.PowerShell.Utility\Format-Table -AutoSize | Microsoft.PowerShell.Utility\Out-String -Width 120

steps.title: Scan the system drive
args: $ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop'; try { 'Scanning the drive. Windows shows no progress for this, so expect a quiet minute or two.'; $result = Storage\Repair-Volume -DriveLetter $env:SystemDrive.Substring(0, 1) -Scan; "Result: $result"; if ($result -ne 'NoErrorsFound') { exit 1 } } catch { $_.Exception.Message; exit 2 }

items.name: Create a restore point
items.summary: A save point to go back to if something goes wrong after a change. Good to do before repairs or installing drivers.
items.effect: Uses a little disk space. Windows allows one restore point every 24 hours; if one is already there, this says when it was made. If System Protection is off for your system drive, the option below turns it on (it is off by default on many new PCs).
sources: Microsoft Learn: Checkpoint-Computer, Enable-ComputerRestore

options.label: Turn on System Protection for the system drive if it is off
options.detail: Without it Windows cannot make restore points. Nothing changes if it is already on.

steps.title: Turn on System Protection
args: $ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop'; $drive = $env:SystemDrive + '\'; try { Microsoft.PowerShell.Management\Enable-ComputerRestore -Drive $drive; 'System Protection is on for ' + $drive } catch { $_.Exception.Message; exit 1 }

steps.title: Create the restore point
args: $ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop'; try { $before = @(Microsoft.PowerShell.Management\Get-ComputerRestorePoint -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue); $known = @($before | Microsoft.PowerShell.Core\ForEach-Object { $_.SequenceNumber }); Microsoft.PowerShell.Management\Checkpoint-Computer -Description 'TidyWindow restore point' -RestorePointType MODIFY_SETTINGS -WarningVariable skipped -WarningAction SilentlyContinue; $added = @(Microsoft.PowerShell.Management\Get-ComputerRestorePoint -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Microsoft.PowerShell.Core\Where-Object { $known -notcontains $_.SequenceNumber }); if ($added.Count -gt 0) { 'Restore point created.'; exit 0 }; if ($skipped) { "$skipped" }; $latest = $before | Microsoft.PowerShell.Utility\Sort-Object SequenceNumber | Microsoft.PowerShell.Utility\Select-Object -Last 1; if ($latest) { $made = [Management.ManagementDateTimeConverter]::ToDateTime($latest.CreationTime); if (((Microsoft.PowerShell.Utility\Get-Date) - $made).TotalHours -lt 24) { 'No new restore point was needed. Windows allows one every 24 hours, and the one named ' + $latest.Description + ' was made on ' + $made.ToString('f') + '. You can go back to that one.'; exit 0 } }; 'Windows did not create a restore point. System Protection is probably off for the system drive, or the space for restore points is full. Tick the option above to turn it on, or use System Properties > System Protection.'; exit 1 } catch { $_.Exception.Message; exit 2 }

items.name: Fix the clock
items.summary: For a clock that is a few minutes off, which also causes website certificate errors and sign-in problems. Starts the time service and asks the internet to set the time.
items.effect: Only the time is corrected. The time zone is not changed; set it in Settings > Time & language if it is wrong. At the end the output shows which time server Windows is using.
sources: Microsoft Learn: w32tm

options.label: Also reset the time server list
options.detail: Use if syncing fails with “no time data was available”. Sets time.windows.com and pool.ntp.org as the servers. A PC joined to a work or school domain is left alone.

steps.title: Reset the time servers
args: $ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop'; try { if ((CimCmdlets\Get-CimInstance -ClassName Win32_ComputerSystem).PartOfDomain) { 'This PC is joined to a domain, so its time comes from the domain. The time server list was left alone.'; exit 0 }; & "$env:SystemRoot\System32\w32tm.exe" /config '/manualpeerlist:time.windows.com,0x8 pool.ntp.org,0x8' /syncfromflags:manual /update; if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { exit $LASTEXITCODE }; 'Time servers are now time.windows.com and pool.ntp.org.' } catch { $_.Exception.Message; exit 1 }

steps.title: Set the time from the internet
Make sure the Windows Time service is still running
Show where the time comes from

items.name: Rebuild the search index
items.summary: For Windows search that finds nothing, shows old files, or uses a lot of the disk. Deletes the search database (Windows.edb, or Windows.db and its journal files on Windows 11) so Windows builds a fresh one.
items.effect: Search results are incomplete while Windows re-indexes, which can take from a few minutes to over an hour and is quicker when you leave the PC alone.
items.duration: A minute, then Windows indexes in the background
sources: Microsoft Q&A: Windows Search troubleshooting (delete the search database; SetupCompletedSuccessfully)

options.label: Also put the indexed folders back to Windows’ defaults
options.detail: Use if search still misses files you know are there. Folders you added to the index, and folders you excluded from it, go back to Windows’ defaults; set them again in Indexing Options.

steps.title: Reset the list of indexed folders
steps.name: SetupCompletedSuccessfully

items.name: Update Defender and run a quick scan
items.summary: Gets the latest virus definitions and scans the places malware usually hides.
items.effect: Nothing is removed without Defender's own decision. Says so plainly, and stops, if another antivirus has turned Microsoft Defender off. The output ends with the threats on record, or says none were found.
sources: Microsoft Learn: Get-MpComputerStatus, Update-MpSignature, Start-MpScan, Get-MpThreatDetection

options.label: Run a full scan instead of a quick one
options.detail: Reads every file. Can take an hour or more, and the PC may feel slower meanwhile.

steps.title: Check that Defender is the active antivirus
args: $ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop'; try { $s = Defender\Get-MpComputerStatus } catch { 'Microsoft Defender did not answer: ' + $_.Exception.Message + ' Another antivirus has probably taken over, and this fix cannot work.'; exit 2 }; if (-not $s.AMServiceEnabled -or $s.AMRunningMode -eq 'Not running') { 'Microsoft Defender is turned off, usually because another antivirus is installed. Scan with that one instead.'; exit 2 }; 'Defender mode: ' + $s.AMRunningMode; 'Real-time protection: ' + $s.RealTimeProtectionEnabled; 'Definitions: ' + $s.AntivirusSignatureVersion + ', ' + $s.AntivirusSignatureAge + ' day(s) old'; if ($s.AMRunningMode -ne 'Normal') { 'Defender is not the main antivirus here. A scan you start yourself still runs.' }

steps.title: Show what Defender found
args: $ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop'; $threats = @(Defender\Get-MpThreat); if ($threats.Count -eq 0) { 'No threats were found.'; exit 0 }; "$($threats.Count) threat(s) on record:"; $threats | Microsoft.PowerShell.Utility\Select-Object ThreatName, IsActive | Microsoft.PowerShell.Utility\Format-Table -AutoSize | Microsoft.PowerShell.Utility\Out-String -Width 120; $found = @(Defender\Get-MpThreatDetection | Microsoft.PowerShell.Utility\Sort-Object InitialDetectionTime -Descending | Microsoft.PowerShell.Utility\Select-Object -First 10); if ($found.Count -gt 0) { 'Most recent detections:'; $found | Microsoft.PowerShell.Utility\Select-Object InitialDetectionTime, ActionSuccess, @{ Name = 'Files'; Expression = { $_.Resources -join '; ' } } | Microsoft.PowerShell.Utility\Format-Table -Wrap -AutoSize | Microsoft.PowerShell.Utility\Out-String -Width 160 }; if (@($threats | Microsoft.PowerShell.Core\Where-Object { $_.IsActive }).Count -gt 0) { 'Some threats are still active. Open Windows Security to remove them.'; exit 1 }

items.name: Refresh the network connection
items.summary: For websites that will not load while others work, or after switching networks. Clears the saved addresses Windows remembers and optionally asks the router for a new one.
items.effect: Your connection may drop for a few seconds. Nothing is reset to defaults, so settings such as a fixed IP address are kept.
sources: Microsoft Support: Fix network connection issues
WinUtil (cross-check)

options.label: Ask the router for a new IP address
options.detail: The usual fix for “connected, no internet”.

options.label: Restart the network adapters
options.detail: Disconnects Wi-Fi and Ethernet for a few seconds.

items.name: Reset the network stack
items.summary: For when Refresh did not help: no internet on any app, or network adapters that are missing or stuck. Puts Windows' network settings back to their defaults.
items.effect: A fixed IP address, custom DNS servers or a manually set proxy may need to be entered again, and VPN software may need reinstalling. Needs a restart to finish.
sources: Microsoft Support: Fix network connection issues (Winsock and TCP/IP reset)
WinUtil (cross-check)

options.label: Also clear the system proxy
options.detail: Use if a proxy you do not use is blocking the connection.

items.name: Clear stuck print jobs
items.summary: For a printer that says “printing” forever, or documents that cannot be cancelled. Stops the print service, empties the print queue and starts it again.
items.effect: All waiting print jobs are cancelled. Printers and their drivers are not touched.
sources: Microsoft Support: Printer spooler troubleshooting (clear the PRINTERS folder)

items.name: Restart sound services
items.summary: For no sound, crackling, or a speaker or headset that Windows does not see. Restarts the services that run audio.
items.effect: Sound stops for a few seconds, and apps playing audio may need to be restarted.
sources: Microsoft Support: Fix sound or audio problems

options.label: Also restart Bluetooth support
options.detail: Bluetooth devices disconnect for a moment and reconnect by themselves.

items.name: Restart Bluetooth
items.summary: For Bluetooth headphones, a mouse or a keyboard that shows as connected but does nothing, or will not pair. Restarts the Bluetooth service.
items.effect: Bluetooth devices disconnect for a moment and reconnect by themselves. Nothing is unpaired.
sources: Microsoft Support: Fix Bluetooth problems in Windows

items.name: Rescan hardware
items.summary: For a USB device, drive or dock that was plugged in but does not show up. Asks Windows to look for hardware changes, like Device Manager's Scan button.
items.effect: Nothing is removed or changed; devices Windows finds are set up as usual.
sources: Microsoft Learn: PnPUtil /scan-devices

items.name: Reset Microsoft Store
items.summary: For a Store that will not open, loads forever, or fails to download or update apps.
items.effect: Clears the Store's cache. You stay signed in and keep your apps. The Store opens by itself when the reset finishes. Windows requires administrator permission for this tool.
sources: Microsoft Support: Reset the Microsoft Store cache (WSReset)

items.name: Fix Start menu and taskbar
items.summary: For a Start menu or search box that will not open, a blank or frozen taskbar, or a Settings app that closes at once. Registers Windows' own shell apps again.
items.effect: The taskbar disappears for a few seconds while File Explorer restarts. Your pinned items and settings are kept.
sources: Microsoft Q&A: Start menu not working (re-register the shell packages, including the Windows 11 shell components)

steps.title: Register the Start menu, taskbar, search and Settings apps again
args: $ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop'; $hosts = 'ShellExperienceHost', 'StartMenuExperienceHost', 'SearchApp', 'SearchUI', 'SearchHost', 'SystemSettings'; $failed = @(); $core = 'Microsoft.Windows.ShellExperienceHost', 'Microsoft.Windows.StartMenuExperienceHost', 'windows.immersivecontrolpanel'; foreach ($name in $core + 'Microsoft.UI.Xaml.CBS', 'MicrosoftWindows.Client.Core', 'MicrosoftWindows.Client.CBS') { $packages = @(Appx\Get-AppxPackage -Name $name | Microsoft.PowerShell.Core\Where-Object { $_ }); if ($packages.Count -eq 0) { "$name is not installed."; continue }; foreach ($package in $packages) { $manifest = Microsoft.PowerShell.Management\Join-Path $package.InstallLocation 'AppXManifest.xml'; $done = $false; $reason = ''; foreach ($attempt in 1, 2) { try { Appx\Add-AppxPackage -DisableDevelopmentMode -ForceApplicationShutdown -Register $manifest; $done = $true; break } catch { $reason = $_.Exception.Message.Split([char]10)[0].Trim(); if ($attempt -eq 1) { "$name is in use. Closing it so Windows can open it again, then trying once more."; Microsoft.PowerShell.Management\Get-Process -Name $hosts -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Microsoft.PowerShell.Management\Stop-Process -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue; Microsoft.PowerShell.Utility\Start-Sleep -Seconds 3 } } }; if ($done) { "Registered $name." } else { if ($core -contains $name) { $failed += $name }; "Could not register $name. $reason" } } }; if ($failed.Count -gt 0) { throw ('Could not register: ' + (($failed | Microsoft.PowerShell.Utility\Select-Object -Unique) -join ', ') + '. Restart Windows and run this fix again.') }

items.name: Fix wrong or blank icons
items.summary: For icons that show the wrong picture, a plain white page, or thumbnails that never appear. Deletes the saved icon pictures so Windows draws them fresh.
items.effect: The taskbar and desktop disappear for a few seconds, and folders may be slow to show thumbnails the first time afterwards.
sources: Microsoft Q&A: Rebuild the icon cache

steps.title: Delete the saved icons and thumbnails

items.name: Reset OneDrive
items.summary: For OneDrive that is stuck syncing, shows the wrong status, or will not start. Resets the sync app without touching your files.
items.effect: OneDrive is closed, reset and started again (this waits about 20 seconds to see whether it started by itself). It then checks all its files again, which can take a while. No files are deleted.
items.duration: A minute, then OneDrive syncs again
sources: Microsoft Support: Reset OneDrive

steps.title: Start OneDrive again if it did not start by itself
args: $ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop'; Microsoft.PowerShell.Utility\Start-Sleep -Seconds 20; if (Microsoft.PowerShell.Management\Get-Process -Name OneDrive -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue) { 'OneDrive is running.' } else { $path = @("$env:LOCALAPPDATA\Microsoft\OneDrive\OneDrive.exe", "$env:ProgramFiles\Microsoft OneDrive\OneDrive.exe", "${env:ProgramFiles(x86)}\Microsoft OneDrive\OneDrive.exe") | Microsoft.PowerShell.Core\Where-Object { Microsoft.PowerShell.Management\Test-Path $_ } | Microsoft.PowerShell.Utility\Select-Object -First 1; if (-not $path) { throw 'OneDrive was not found.' }; 'OneDrive did not start by itself. Starting it now.'; Microsoft.PowerShell.Management\Start-Process -FilePath $path -ArgumentList '/background' }

items.name: Rebuild the font cache
items.summary: For text that shows empty boxes or garbled letters, fonts that are missing from apps, or apps that freeze while loading fonts. Deletes the saved font database so Windows builds a fresh one.
items.effect: Apps may be slow for a moment the first time they load fonts afterwards. Installed fonts are not removed. Restart open apps (or Windows) for the new cache to be used everywhere. The old system file FNTCACHE.DAT is kept open by Windows while you are signed in; if so it is left and the output says so.
sources: Microsoft Q&A: Fonts display as boxes or are missing (stop Windows Font Cache Service, delete the cache files, start it again)

steps.title: Stop the WPF font cache service
Delete the old system font cache file
Start the WPF font cache service

items.name: Check and repair WMI
items.summary: For tools that fail with “Invalid namespace”, error 0x80041002 or WMI timeouts: system information, hardware readouts, some installers and games. Checks the WMI repository, repairs it if it is inconsistent, and then asks WMI a question to prove it answers.
items.effect: The check changes nothing. The repair keeps everything it can still read and drops only what is damaged; programs that registered their own WMI parts may need to be repaired or reinstalled if they stop working. The repository is never wiped.
sources: Microsoft Learn: WMI troubleshooting (winmgmt /verifyrepository, then /salvagerepository, verify again, then test a query)

options.label: Repair the repository if it is inconsistent
options.detail: Leave this off to only check it.

steps.title: Ask WMI a question
args: $ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop'; try { $os = CimCmdlets\Get-CimInstance -ClassName Win32_OperatingSystem; 'WMI answered: ' + $os.Caption + ' ' + $os.Version } catch { 'WMI did not answer a simple question: ' + $_.Exception.Message; exit 1 }

items.name: Fix blank Task Manager graphs and counters
items.summary: For Task Manager or Resource Monitor showing blank or zero graphs, Performance Monitor saying “Unable to add these counters”, or games and monitoring tools that cannot read CPU, disk or GPU figures. Rebuilds the performance counter list from Windows’ own backup.
items.effect: Nothing you own is touched. Counters that a program added after Windows last saved its backup come back when that program is repaired or reinstalled. Open Task Manager again afterwards; a restart may be needed.
sources: Microsoft Learn: lodctr /R (rebuild counter settings from the system backup store); winmgmt /resyncperf

steps.title: Tell WMI about the counters again
Check that the counters answer
args: $ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop'; try { $sets = @(Microsoft.PowerShell.Diagnostics\Get-Counter -ListSet *); if ($sets.Count -eq 0) { 'Windows lists no performance counters.'; exit 1 }; 'Windows lists ' + $sets.Count + ' performance counter sets.' } catch { 'The counters do not answer yet: ' + $_.Exception.Message + ' Restart Windows and check Task Manager again.'; exit 1 }

items.name: Find out why the PC will not sleep
items.summary: For a PC that will not go to sleep, wakes up by itself in the night, or fails to resume. Shows what is keeping it awake, what woke it last and which devices may wake it. Can also rebuild the hibernation file or put the power plans back to Windows’ own.
items.effect: The reports change nothing. Rebuilding the hibernation file only happens if hibernation is on, and makes the file at its default size. Putting the power plans back deletes custom plans, including the ones from the PC maker.
sources: Microsoft Learn: powercfg command-line options (/requests, /lastwake, /devicequery, /hibernate, -restoredefaultschemes)

options.label: Rebuild the hibernation file (used by Fast Startup)
options.detail: Use if resuming from hibernation or starting the PC hangs. Skipped if hibernation is turned off.

options.label: Put the power plans back to Windows’ defaults
options.detail: Deletes custom power plans, including ones set up by the PC maker or by you.

steps.title: Show the sleep states this PC supports
Show what is keeping the PC awake
Show what woke the PC last
Show the devices that may wake the PC
Rebuild the hibernation file
args: $ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop'; $power = "$env:SystemRoot\System32\powercfg.exe"; $on = (Microsoft.PowerShell.Management\Get-ItemProperty -Path 'HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Power' -Name HibernateEnabled).HibernateEnabled; if ($on -ne 1) { 'Hibernation is turned off on this PC, so it was left off.'; exit 0 }; & $power /hibernate off; $off = $LASTEXITCODE; & $power /hibernate on; $back = $LASTEXITCODE; if ($back -ne 0) { 'Hibernation could not be turned back on. Run powercfg /hibernate on in an administrator terminal.'; exit $back }; if ($off -ne 0) { exit $off }; 'The hibernation file was made again.'

steps.title: Put the power plans back to defaults

items.name: Fix other PCs not showing in Network
items.summary: For a home or office network where other PCs, a NAS or shared folders do not appear under Network in File Explorer. Restarts the services Windows uses to find and announce devices.
items.effect: Network browsing may pause for a few seconds. Firewall and sharing settings are not changed: if devices still do not show, turn on Network discovery in Settings > Network & internet > Advanced network settings > Advanced sharing settings.
sources: Microsoft Support: Network discovery (Function Discovery services must be running)

items.name: Restart the camera service
items.summary: For a webcam that says “in use by another app” or “no camera found”, often after a video call ended badly. Restarts the service that shares the camera between apps and looks for the camera again.
items.effect: Any app using the camera loses it and may need to be reopened. Nothing is changed or removed.
sources: Microsoft Support: Camera does not work in Windows (Windows Camera Frame Server)

steps.title: Stop the Windows Camera Frame Server
Start the Windows Camera Frame Server

items.name: Find devices with problems
items.summary: For a USB, Bluetooth, audio or other device that Device Manager marks with a yellow warning, or that stopped working after sleep. Lists every device that reports an error and its code.
items.effect: Nothing is changed; this only reads and reports. It finishes with a warning when it finds devices, so you can see them in the output. Use Rescan hardware, reinstall the driver from the maker, or look the code up in Device Manager.
sources: Microsoft Learn: Get-PnpDevice

steps.title: List devices that report a problem
args: $ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop'; $bad = @(PnpDevice\Get-PnpDevice -PresentOnly | Microsoft.PowerShell.Core\Where-Object { $_.Status -in 'Error', 'Degraded' -or [int]$_.ConfigManagerErrorCode -ne 0 }); if ($bad.Count -eq 0) { 'No device reports a problem.' } else { "$($bad.Count) device(s) report a problem:"; $bad | Microsoft.PowerShell.Utility\Select-Object FriendlyName, Class, Status, @{ Name = 'Code'; Expression = { [int]$_.ConfigManagerErrorCode } }, @{ Name = 'Meaning'; Expression = { "$($_.ConfigManagerErrorCode)" } } | Microsoft.PowerShell.Utility\Format-Table -AutoSize | Microsoft.PowerShell.Utility\Out-String -Width 160; exit 1 }

items.name: Fix a blank Windows Security window
items.summary: For Windows Security that opens blank, closes at once, or says you need a new app to open the windowsdefender link. Registers the Windows Security app again and resets its app data.
items.effect: Only the Windows Security app is repaired. Your virus protection settings and exclusions belong to Microsoft Defender and are kept. If another antivirus has taken over, Windows Security shows less.
sources: Microsoft Q&A: Windows Security app blank or not opening (re-register Microsoft.SecHealthUI, Reset-AppxPackage)

steps.title: Register the Windows Security app again
args: $ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop'; $package = Appx\Get-AppxPackage -Name Microsoft.SecHealthUI | Microsoft.PowerShell.Utility\Select-Object -First 1; if (-not $package) { throw 'The Windows Security app is not installed for this account.' }; Appx\Add-AppxPackage -DisableDevelopmentMode -ForceApplicationShutdown -Register (Microsoft.PowerShell.Management\Join-Path $package.InstallLocation 'AppXManifest.xml'); 'Registered ' + $package.Name + ' ' + $package.Version + '.'

steps.title: Reset the Windows Security app data

items.name: Repair WinGet and App Installer
items.summary: For winget that stopped working after an update, or fails with “Data required by the source is missing” (0x8a15000f). Registers App Installer again and refreshes winget’s app lists.
items.effect: Nothing you installed is touched. If the source error stays, open an administrator terminal and run winget source reset --force, which Windows only allows for administrators.
sources: Microsoft Learn: winget source (update); Microsoft Q&A: Re-register App Installer

steps.title: Register App Installer again
args: $ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop'; $package = Appx\Get-AppxPackage -Name Microsoft.DesktopAppInstaller | Microsoft.PowerShell.Utility\Select-Object -First 1; if (-not $package) { throw 'App Installer is not installed for this account. Install or update it from the Microsoft Store.' }; Appx\Add-AppxPackage -DisableDevelopmentMode -ForceApplicationShutdown -Register (Microsoft.PowerShell.Management\Join-Path $package.InstallLocation 'AppXManifest.xml'); 'Registered ' + $package.Name + ' ' + $package.Version + '.'
